extracted.intended_audience: astronomers, natural philosophers, and Royal Society members (17th‑century observational scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Protocols and practical criteria for making, recording, and reporting telescopic astronomical observations (eclipses, planetary/satellite configurations, and related measurements), including instrument specification, timekeeping, comparison with tables, and presentation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report instrument specification and observer metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: State the observing location (latitude and longitude), the observers' names, the instruments used (tube/telescope lengths), and which micrometer or sight was employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Flamsteed reports two tubes (one 19(64)-inches long with Townly's micrometer and one 10(3/4)-inches with his own), lists assistants (Mr. Halley), and gives locations (Dantzic, Townly, Derby, Paris) and lat./long. for observations. Include which observer used which instrument when reporting measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record raw clock times and apply explicit corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Record time by the observing clock (e.g., pendulum clock) and then give corrected times, stating the correction method and magnitude (e.g., meridian line or sun-dial corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed and others tabulate 'Time by the Pend. Clock' and 'Corrected Time.' Note examples where a clock is found too slow by 1m 42s (meridian line correction) but only 45s by a sun-dial; state which correction is trusted and why (author preferred meridian-line correction over sun-dial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and report eclipse phases and angular measures precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Give times for beginning, greatest obscuration, end, duration, and provide angular measures such as sun's semidiameter, moon's semidiameter, quantity (degrees, minutes, seconds), and 'digits eclipsed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate phase times and corresponding measured values in arc (examples include 'Sun's dia. 6360 = 31' 43"' and semidiameters like '4° 21' 30"'). Provide measures from different instruments (long vs short telescope) for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple instruments/observers and attribute specific measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, use more than one tube/telescope and more than one observer to measure complementary quantities (e.g., one measures azimuth distances while another measures lucid parts and cusps) and explicitly state which data came from which instrument and observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed: two tubes prepared, one observer took measures of first eight phases, the other took distances of azimuths and cusps; record such division of labor and compare results to assess instrument suitability (e.g., one micrometer 'fitter for this use than the other').

rubrics_metrics.name: Document observational conditions and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Record sky conditions (clouds, sun emerging/hidden, visibility of limb) and note how these affected the observation or whether parts were obscured or clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text note 'No eclipse yet. Clouds', 'Sun then hid by clouds', or 'The limb seen through the clouds appeared free from the eclipse.' Indicate when measures may be less reliable due to clouds or poor seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present results with figures/plates and tabular data references
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish measurements and sequences together with referenced figures and plates (e.g., fig. 1, pl. 10) and present data in tables for each phase/measure for clarity and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple entries reference 'see the type at fig. 1, pi. 10' and present step-by-step tables of times and corrected times; include plate/figure numbers when describing geometrical constructions or measured features (cusps, horns, azimuths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observations against astronomical tables and cross‑location data
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare observed event times and measures with computed tables (e.g., Rudolphine Tables) and with observations from other locations/observers to identify differences and validate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives observed times alongside 'Calcul. by the Rudolphine Table' and reports observations from Dantzic, Townly, Halton, Paris, etc.; provide differences and minutes of discrepancy to assess accuracy and to refine predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer measuring and correcting with meridian‑based methods when available
rubrics_metrics.description: When precise daily time correction is needed, prefer meridian-line (transit) corrections to sun-dial corrections for clock calibration, and state the reason for preferring one correction over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed notes trusting the correction by the meridian line rather than the sun-dial because the meridian line indicated the clock was too slow by 1m 42s whereas the sun-dial gave ~45s; explicitly state such preferences and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use eclipses and satellite configurations to test and refine hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Make repeated, careful observations of satellite configurations and eclipses across seasons/years to verify orbital hypotheses (nodes, obliquity, inversion of circles), separating proper motions of satellites from apparent effects caused by the planet's motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cassini advises astronomers to observe configurations occurring rarely (twice in 12 years) with care to verify hypotheses; he lists predicted phenomena (e.g., satellites lining up, eclipsing each other, inversion of semicircles) and argues eclipses are key tests that distinguish competing systems (Galileo, Marius, Cassini).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account theoretically for observational appearance (separate proper from apparent motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In interpreting observations, explicitly consider and separate the satellites' proper motion from apparent appearances produced by the primary planet's motion about the sun and by geometrical projection effects (inclination/obliquity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cassini criticizes prior hypotheses for not separating proper motion from appearances caused by Jupiter's motion; he shows this omission leads to large errors in predicted eclipse timings and configurations—hence include such separation in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: State explicit modeling assumptions when deriving orbital elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When deriving aphelia, eccentricities, or orbital proportions, state and rely only on explicit assumptions (e.g., orbits are elliptical, sun in common focus, periods known accurately), and make the parallax-of-orbit (annual motion of Earth) the basis for certain optical inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley's 'Direct and Geometrical Method' begins by assuming elliptical orbits, sun at focus, and sufficiently known periods (no sensible error in 2–3 revolutions), and uses Earth-orbit parallax as a solid basis for the method; state such assumptions up front and indicate expected limits of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide functional design requirements for apparatus (example: hydraulic engine)
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a mechanical design intended for practical use, state the required functional behavior (e.g., maintain continuous jet even when pump action ceases) and explain the mechanism achieving it (e.g., compressed‑air vessel with valves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hydraulic engine description specifies that the jet must continue when pump's sucker ceases, achieved by a copper vessel communicating with the pump that compresses air and drives water out; detail the valves, tubes, and sequence of operation so others can reproduce or judge the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose pedagogical or scientific qualities of good experimental writing
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviews of experimental works, value clarity (an 'intelligible account'), breadth of specimens/examples, mechanical explanations for observed qualities, and the inclusion of experiments and reflections that supply materials for further history or theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review of Boyle praises his clear, varied specimens and mechanical explanations of qualities (heat/cold, tastes/odours, volatility/fixity), and notes additions like notes on magnetism and electricity. Use such criteria when assessing experimental publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document extraordinary empirical cases with detailed revival procedures and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting medical-rescue or extraordinary survival cases, provide the sequence of interventions, precautions taken, and contextual remarks or skepticism/limits from later knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account of a Swedish gardener revived after 16 hours lists wrapping to prevent sudden air rush, gradual warming, rubbing/rolling, and administration of spirituous liquor; the author also appends a modern caveat that drowning victims are destroyed by suppression of respiration—include such caveats and provenance (attestation by reputable witnesses).
